units.title: OP Stack chains with ETH gas
angles: Arithmetic and control flow. Read the interpreter this network runs at the release its endpoint reports, and any compiler, bytecode rewriting, caching or code analysis stage in front of it. Cover the 256 bit integer library and its pinned version, MULMOD, ADDMOD, DIV, SDIV, MOD, SMOD, SIGNEXTEND, SAR, SHL, SHR, BYTE, EXP, the comparisons, JUMP and JUMPI with the jump destination analysis, KECCAK256, MCOPY, memory expansion and CALLDATALOAD. Compare each with the Ethereum specification at the edges that OPCODES.md lists, and read the release notes and fix commits since the versions OPCODES.md records. Then rerun the scripts in research/network-risk/tools/opdiff (battery.py, targeted.py, pmdiff.py, pmdiff2.py, swaps.py, replay.py) for this unit's chain ids, write the outputs into your work directory, and add vectors for anything the reading makes suspicious. Report every result that differs from the specification, every release that changed these paths, how a wrong result would change the pool math in src/libraries (TickMath, BitMath, FullMath, SqrtPriceMath, SwapMath, TickBitmap) or the logic that depends on it, and which validators could run a different code path than the public endpoint.

Upcoming forks. Assume every network upgrade scheduled or proposed for the next six months ships. What changes for the PoolManager and for funds already inside it, and what could an ordinary account do the day after?

code.title: theme-outflow-census
code.task: The build of this checkout is in research/network-risk/build/PoolManager.json (runtime 24,009 bytes), research/network-risk/tools/opdiff/pyevm.py is a reference EVM in Python, research/network-risk/tools/opdiff/v4math.py is a transcription of the math libraries, research/network-risk/opcodes/jumpmap.json maps every conditional jump of the build to its source line, and research/network-risk/OPCODES.md holds what is already tested and read, with sections on what cycles 10 to 21 added and a list of what is not covered. Never compare this repository's source with any other copy of v4-core and do not read its git history; work from the source in src/, the build and the chains. Read-only RPC only, no transactions. Do not install software. Python 3, rustc 1.97 with cargo, go 1.24, node and the system C and C++ compilers are present, and you may compile downloaded source inside your own work directory. Keep downloads and build output under a directory named build/ or dl/ inside your work directory. Do not download compiler toolchains or other binaries to run them; source archives are fine. Record every sampling seed, save every mismatch record in full, and bracket each batch of calls to a public endpoint with web3_clientVersion so the build that answered is known. If an endpoint refuses your client (HTTP 403, 429 or a challenge page), record that and use another public endpoint; do not try to get around the refusal and use no API keys. Analysis only: no exploit code and no transactions. Leads L-965 and L-975. A use of any weakness that takes funds leaves a mined record, whatever opcode, precompile or system path it rides on: a currency leaves the PoolManager, or claims are minted, and no pool event of that transaction pays for it. The only census of that kind is from cycle 6 (research/network-risk/cycles/006/theme-currency-lists.work, scripts census2.py and raw/census_summary.json). It covered 3 days on Base, 5 days on Robinhood Chain, 14 days on Ethereum, Ink and X Layer, up to 60 days elsewhere, and full history only on Zora, Celo and Elysium. Later variants are in research/network-risk/cycles/018/theme-sync-leak-census.work and research/network-risk/cycles/019/theme-census-endpoints.work (census.py, gapcheck2.py). Task 1: read those scripts and write down the rule exactly as they apply it: per transaction and currency, logged ERC-20 outflow from the PoolManager plus ERC-6909 claims minted, minus inflow and claims burned, against the Swap, ModifyLiquidity and Donate amounts, hook deltas and protocol fee collection of that transaction. Say how the native currency is handled, since native transfers leave no log, and name what the rule cannot see. Task 2: before each range on each endpoint run gapcheck2.py, and do not use an endpoint that answers an old range with an empty list and no error (reth-bsc on publicnode does this below block 135,500,000, finding F-142). Record endpoint, client version, block range and log counts. Task 3: extend the census from the PoolManager deployment block to the current head, in this order: Base, Robinhood Chain, Ethereum, Ink, X Layer, then Arbitrum One, OP Mainnet, Unichain and the rest as time allows. If a full history is beyond what public endpoints give, cover the newest contiguous range you can reach and one oldest range from the deployment block, and state exactly which block ranges are covered and which are not. Do not sample silently. Task 4: for every transaction the rule cannot explain, classify it. Either it belongs to a recorded finding (rebasing and balance-raising tokens such as F-012, F-041, F-066, F-067, F-079, fee-on-transfer tokens, hook fee ledgers such as F-084) and you name which, or it is unexplained. List each unexplained transaction in full with its hash, block, currency, amounts and the PoolManager functions called, and trace it where an endpoint serves traces. Task 5 (L-975): list which earlier clearances and findings (for example the F-091 and F-112 transaction counts and the BNB Chain transfer census) rest on eth_getLogs answers for ranges where the endpoint used fails gapcheck2, on BNB Chain, Ethereum and Polygon.

Keep downloads and build output under a directory named build/ or dl/ inside your work directory. Do not download compiler toolchains or other binaries to run them; source archives are fine. Record every sampling seed, save every mismatch record in full, and bracket each batch of calls to a public endpoint with web3_clientVersion so the build that answered is known. If an endpoint refuses your client (HTTP 403, 429 or a challenge page), record that and use another public endpoint; do not try to get around the refusal and use no API keys. Analysis only: no exploit code and no transactions. Leads L-966, L-960 and L-976. take, settle, settleFor, mint, burn and clear are gated only by the transient flag IS_UNLOCKED (src/PoolManager.sol:96-99), and the only settlement check is the nonzero delta count at the end of unlock (src/PoolManager.sol:112). One fault in transient rollback or transient lifetime on a block producing path would let any account take a currency with no settlement. Cycle 21 tested this with eth_simulateV1 on 16 networks and with eth_call on all 21 (research/network-risk/cycles/021/theme-blind-read.work), but HyperEVM, Arc, MegaETH, Monad, Avalanche and Elysium have no eth_simulateV1, a closed or unpublished producer, or (Monad) compiled code that eth_call never runs. This theme looks at mined blocks on those six. Task 1: find which public endpoints of the six serve debug_traceTransaction with callTracer, trace_transaction or trace_block, and record every refusal. Task 2: over fixed block windows that you record (as much history as the endpoints allow, newest first), take every transaction with a PoolManager log or a token Transfer to or from the PoolManager, fetch its call trace, and list (a) every successful PoolManager frame of take, settle, settleFor, mint, burn, clear, swap, modifyLiquidity or donate with no PoolManager unlock frame above it on the call stack, (b) every transaction in which a PoolManager unlock frame reverts or halts and a later PoolManager frame of those functions in the same transaction succeeds outside a new unlock, and (c) for each transaction that ends with a currency synced and not settled (the cycle 18 census in research/network-risk/cycles/018/theme-sync-leak-census.work has the method), whether the next PoolManager transaction of the same block behaves as if the slots were empty. The expected count for (a) and (b) is zero; report the number of transactions and frames examined per network. Where no endpoint serves traces, apply the weaker log form (a token Transfer out of the PoolManager in a transaction whose top-level call and logs show no path through unlock) and say that it is weaker. Task 3 (L-960, L-976): by reading client source at the revisions the endpoints report, say whether the balance debit for CALLVALUE is enforced on the block execution path where a system path sets the value: Arbitrum retryable redeems (arbos/tx_processor.go at the consensus-v61 commit: is the callvalue taken from the ticket escrow balance in state, and is transient storage empty when the scheduled redeem starts), OP Stack deposits with a mint field, Tempo batched calls, and HyperEVM system transactions. Native settle credits msg.value with no balance comparison (src/PoolManager.sol:353-354), so a path that sets CALLVALUE without a debit would mint native credit.

Cycle 21 (research/network-risk/cycles/021/theme-ruint-releases.work) found three ruint faults that are off the opcode handler path: release 1.19.0 truncates shift amounts of 2^32 or more modulo 2^32 (linked by Base v1.5.6 and MegaETH), releases 1.18.0 and 1.19.0 return a wrong overflowing_shl flag (X Layer links 1.18.0), and every release up to 1.21.1 zero extends negative values in wrapping_from, saturating_from and the signed TryFrom (#701, #704). Only the EVM instruction handlers were shown not to reach them. Balances of precompile tokens that the PoolManager holds are computed in Rust and not by EVM opcodes, so a wrong shift or conversion there would change a pooled balance with every opcode correct. Task 1 (L-967): at the tags the endpoints report, list every call site in the Rust-native precompiles and system contracts of Base v1.5.6 (the B20 token precompiles, factory and policy registry), mega-evm v1.7.4 (system contracts and limit accounting) and xlayer v0.0.7 that calls ruint Shl or Shr with a primitive integer amount, uses the overflowing_shl flag, or converts a signed value with wrapping_from, saturating_from or TryFrom. For each give the range its amount or operand can take and whether a faulty input is reachable by an ordinary account. Task 2 (L-968): the same search for the Tempo precompiles at a9d6748 (tip20/mod.rs, tip20/rewards.rs, stablecoin_dex/mod.rs, tip_fee_manager/amm.rs, tip20_channel_reserve/mod.rs), the Arc native coin precompiles of arc-node v0.8.6 and the HyperEVM read precompiles in nanoreth nb-20261125-2. stablecoin_dex/mod.rs near line 2059 does signed tick arithmetic for prices; say whether a negative value can reach a U256 conversion there. Where a site looks reachable, test it by eth_call on the network against the value the arithmetic should give. Task 3 (L-969): at tempo a9d6748, and at the T14 release tag if one is published, re-read every caller of TIP20Token::system_transfer_from and channel_reserve_transfer. system_transfer_from pulls TIP-20 tokens with no allowance and leaves the choice of account to each call site (tip20/mod.rs lines 945-958). In TIP20ChannelReserve, can an ordinary account open, fund or capture a channel in which the PoolManager is the payer, or make receive_policy_sender differ from the account whose balance moves (tip20/mod.rs lines 997-1010), without the PoolManager itself calling the reserve? The PoolManager on Tempo is 0x33620f62c5b9b2086dd6b62f4a297a9f30347029.

Analysis only: no exploit code and no transactions. Lead L-970, which carries the rest of L-101. Any L1 account can send a deposit to an OP Stack chain, and a deposit that fails still commits its nonce and mint. A handler that commits a failed deposit without clearing transient storage would carry PoolManager transient slots (the unlock flag, the delta count, the synced currency and reserves: src/libraries/Lock.sol, NonzeroDeltaCount.sol, CurrencyReserves.sol, CurrencyDelta.sol) into the next transaction of the block. The cycle 21 critic read op-revm in op-reth v2.10.0-rc.4 (rust/op-revm/src/handler.rs lines 408-535): a halted deposit is sent to catch_error_failed_deposit, which reverts to the first checkpoint and then calls commit_tx, and revm-context 43.0.3 clears transient storage in commit_tx and discard_tx (src/journal/inner.rs lines 141-158 and 174-192). Task 1: do the same reading for the builds with their own handler code, at the revisions the endpoints report today: Base reth/v2.5.2 base/v1.5.6, conduit-op-reth v2.5.1 (Zora), world-chain v2.8.2, celo-reth v2.2.0, xlayer v0.0.7 on reth v2.3.0, and mega-evm v1.7.4 (MegaETH). For each, quote the lines where a failed or halted deposit is handled and where transient storage is cleared, with the revm-context version pinned in its Cargo.lock. Task 2: on each of those builds list every EVM execution that runs outside a user transaction's own frame: the L1 attributes deposit, EIP-4788 and EIP-2935 system calls, Celo fee currency debit and credit calls (CIP-64), Base phase loops if the reported build has them, and MegaETH system contracts. For each say whether transient storage is cleared between it and the neighbouring transaction, and whether an ordinary account can make it call code that the account chose. Task 3: check the reading against mined blocks. Find mined deposits that failed or halted on these chains (receipt status 0 with type 0x7e) and that were followed in the same block by a PoolManager transaction, and confirm from receipts and, where served, traces that the later transaction behaved as with empty transient slots. Report how many such pairs each chain has in the windows you could read, and record the windows.

Run gapcheck2.py (research/network-risk/cycles/019/theme-census-endpoints.work) on each log endpoint first and record ranges. For each such pool give the flag bits, the pool's liquidity, the PoolManager balance attributable to it where it can be estimated, and whether any position was added by an account other than the pool's creating account (ModifyLiquidity senders and, for the PositionManager, token owners). Task 3: for each pool where bits 9, 8, 5 or 4 are set and third-party liquidity exists, say who can place code at the hook address: is it the output of a known deterministic factory (CREATE2 deployer 0x4e59b44847b379578588920ca78fbf26c0b4956c, CreateX, or a launch pad factory) whose init code or salt lets an account other than the pool creator deploy there, or an address with a nonce or signed transactions (a key holder who can delegate under EIP-7702 on the networks that have it). Say on which of the 21 networks an address without code does not answer a call with success and empty data (reserved or native-code address ranges such as the ones in F-139, F-125 and F-127), since the behaviour of an empty hook differs there. Analysis only: do not deploy anything and do not send transactions.
